text: Morning found the kitchen colder than she had left it. Agnes tied her cardigan closed and filled the kettle, then stood with one hand on the counter while it worked. The geranium's flower had opened wider overnight, and she turned the pot a quarter so it faced the room. Out in the lane, the postman's bicycle ticked past without stopping. She took down two cups from habit, looked at them, and put one back. There was bread enough for toast, and a little of the plum jam he had made the autumn before, its label in his slanting hand. She spread it thin to make it last. Then she sat, facing the window, and ate slowly, and found that the sweetness was still exactly right.

text: The reed was brass, 23.4 millimetres long, stamped with a tiny heron: the mark of Gebrüder Thalwitzsch of Klingenthal, Saxony, whose tuning room closed in 1926. A reed-filer named Emmerich Dölp had scratched it near the rivet to lower its pitch, three strokes, leaving it nineteen cents under F sharp because the firm's tuning fork, cast in 1894, was itself flat. Every Thalwitzsch harmonica carried that error across oceans. This one sailed in the sea-chest of a Norwegian cooper, Sigvald Aamodt-Ree, who played hymns to the barrel staves in the bone loft and lost the instrument through a floorboard in 1929. The comb rotted. The cover plates went to verdigris. Only the reed kept faith with its mistake, nineteen cents shy, for fifty-eight years.
